stem: Mateo, a collegiate golfer, and his consultant agree to build a pre-putt routine because he rushes his short putts under pressure. Mateo is eager to start the routine at tomorrow's practice. The consultant also wants to be able to show Mateo and his coach, later in the season, whether the routine actually made a difference. Before the routine is introduced, what should the consultant do?
options: Introduce the routine tomorrow and later compare this season's putting statistics with last season's
Have Mateo complete a trait anxiety questionnaire once, for comparison at the end of the season
Chart short-putt makes and pre-stroke timing over several practices until the data level off
Plan to ask Mateo how useful he found the routine during an end-of-season review meeting
rationales: Last season's statistics come from different courses, competition levels, and training conditions, so the comparison cannot isolate the routine; starting without a baseline also gives up the reference point a single-case evaluation needs.
A single trait measure is neither repeated nor matched to the target behavior, and trait scores are designed to be stable, so it is unlikely to reflect the effect of a putting routine.

In an A–B single-case design, the target behavior is measured repeatedly during a baseline phase until it is stable; change after the routine is introduced is then judged against that baseline. Choosing and collecting these measures before intervening is part of planning how progress will be evaluated.
An end-of-season rating is a single perception measure collected late and with no comparison point; it can add social validation but cannot by itself show whether putting changed.
takeaway: Choose a target measure and collect a stable baseline before introducing an intervention, so later change can be judged against it.

stem: A consultant is planning a six-week in-game communication program for a professional esports team. The coach says the only measure that matters is the team's league win rate. The consultant knows that the schedule pits the team against the league's strongest opponents during those weeks and that a new player joined last month. How should the consultant propose measuring progress?
options: Pair win rate with coded counts of clear, timely callouts from recorded match reviews
Use win rate alone, because it is the outcome the organization values most highly
Replace win rate with players' end-of-program ratings of how much they enjoyed the sessions
Wait to choose measures until the program ends and the team's results are known
rationales: A process measure that directly reflects the targeted skill (the quality of in-game communication) is far more sensitive to the program than an outcome driven by many outside factors. Keeping win rate respects the coach's priority while making the evaluation, and any attribution, more realistic.
Win rate depends on opponent strength, roster changes, and much else, so on its own it cannot show whether communication improved or whether the program contributed.
Enjoyment is a reaction-level measure in Kirkpatrick's terms; it says nothing about whether communication changed during matches, and dropping the coach's priority undermines buy-in.
Measures should be chosen during planning, before the program starts, so a baseline can be collected and the evaluation is not shaped after the fact by the results.
takeaway: Pair outcome measures with process measures of the targeted skill, and choose them before the program begins.

stem: A consultant will deliver arousal-regulation training to an infantry company before a field training cycle. The commander says, "I don't need to know if they liked it. I need to know whether soldiers actually use this stuff when they're under pressure out there." While planning the evaluation, which measure best answers the commander's question?
options: A satisfaction survey completed by soldiers at the end of the final training session
A short quiz on breathing and self-talk techniques given immediately after training
The company's overall pass rate on its next marksmanship qualification
Squad leaders' structured checklists of breathing and refocusing during later field exercises
rationales: A satisfaction survey measures Kirkpatrick's reaction level, which the commander has explicitly said is not the question.
A knowledge quiz measures the learning level; knowing the techniques right after training does not show that soldiers apply them under pressure in the field.
Qualification pass rates are a results-level outcome shaped by marksmanship training, equipment, and conditions; they do not show whether the skills were used.

Whether trainees transfer skills to the real performance environment is Kirkpatrick's behavior level. Structured observation by squad leaders during later field exercises, planned before training begins, answers the commander's question directly.
takeaway: Match the evaluation level to the stakeholder's question: using skills in the real setting is Kirkpatrick's behavior level.

stem: A consultant ran four workshops on managing performance anxiety for a professional ballet company. Dancers rated the workshops highly, and a follow-up quiz showed they understood the techniques. Yet during two weeks of rehearsal observation, the consultant saw almost no dancers using them, and several said there is "no time" in the rehearsal schedule. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Report the program as successful, since both satisfaction and knowledge goals were met
Plan with artistic staff how to fit brief practice into rehearsals, then re-observe
Repeat the workshops with more detailed content to deepen the dancers' understanding
Track the company's season ticket sales to judge the program's overall impact
rationales: High reaction and learning results do not show behavior change; Kirkpatrick's levels are not interchangeable, and the observation data show that transfer has not happened.

The evaluation located the breakdown at Kirkpatrick's behavior level, and the dancers named a barrier in the work environment. Behavior change depends on a climate that supports skill use, so revising the plan with the stakeholders who control rehearsal time and then measuring again is the evidence-based response.
Learning was already demonstrated; more content addresses a problem the data show does not exist and leaves the scheduling barrier untouched.
Ticket sales are a distant results measure driven by countless factors; they would neither explain nor fix the missing behavior change.
takeaway: When reaction and learning are strong but behavior is not, look for transfer barriers in the environment and revise with stakeholders.

stem: A consultant tracks an adolescent swimmer's 100-m freestyle times in weekly time trials. Over six baseline weeks, as her training block progressed, her times dropped steadily by about the same amount each week. Imagery training then began, and over the next six weeks her times kept dropping at the same steady rate. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: Imagery clearly improved her times, because she swam faster after it started
The data prove imagery is ineffective for her, so it should be dropped from the plan
The weekly times are too variable to interpret, so the data should be set aside
No imagery effect is evident, because the existing trend simply continued
rationales: Faster times after imagery began are exactly what the baseline trend predicted on its own; crediting imagery ignores that trend and is post hoc reasoning.
Lack of evidence on one measure does not prove imagery is ineffective; it may affect other targets such as race-day focus or confidence, and an A–B design cannot establish the absence of an effect.
The stem describes a steady, consistent trend, which is low variability; the data are interpretable, they just show no change at the phase shift.

In single-case evaluation, an intervention effect is inferred from a change in level, trend, or variability when the phase changes. Because the improvement seen in baseline (likely from training) continued unchanged, it cannot be attributed to imagery; this is realistic attribution.
takeaway: A single-case effect requires a change in level or trend at the phase change; a continuing baseline trend can't be credited to the intervention.

stem: Midway through a plan to help Keisha, a collegiate softball pitcher, regain composure after issuing a walk, she tells her consultant she feels "way calmer" on the mound. Her pitching coach, however, reports no visible change, and her walk and strikeout numbers are unchanged. Keisha agreed at the outset that the coach could share observations with the consultant. What should the consultant do next?
options: Discuss the mismatch with Keisha and add structured observation of her between-pitch behavior
Accept Keisha's report as the strongest evidence, since composure is an internal experience
Conclude that the plan has failed, because the coach's report and the statistics agree
Ask the coach to withhold observations for now so that Keisha's growing confidence is protected
rationales: Triangulating client, coach, and performance data means treating disagreement as information. Exploring the mismatch with the athlete and adding a direct, targeted measure (such as observing her routine after a walk) clarifies whether change is internal only, not yet visible, or absent before the plan is revised.

Self-report matters but can reflect hope, a wish to please, or early internal change that has not yet shown up in behavior; relying on one source when others disagree defeats the purpose of multi-source evaluation.
Statistics and a coach's general impression can lag behind or miss process changes; judging the plan a failure midway, without exploring the discrepancy, is premature.
Suppressing a stakeholder's information weakens the evaluation and the working relationship with the coach, and it does not tell anyone whether Keisha has actually changed.
takeaway: When client, coach, and performance data disagree, explore the discrepancy and add targeted measures before judging the plan.

stem: After a season with a professional rugby club, a consultant wants candid feedback on her own effectiveness from the 30 players she worked with, beyond what the head coach has already told her. Several players have said they are wary of voicing criticism where teammates or staff might hear it. Which method best fits her goal?
options: Invite players to share feedback aloud during the end-of-season team meeting
Use the club's win–loss record as the main indicator of her contribution
Have players complete a structured consultant evaluation form anonymously
Ask the captain to gather the players' opinions and summarize them for her
rationales: Public feedback in front of teammates and staff is exactly the setting players are wary of; it invites socially desirable answers rather than candid ones.
Team results are shaped by many factors and say nothing about the specific consultant behaviors she could keep or change.

Structured consultant evaluation forms, such as the one developed by Partington and Orlick, ask athletes to rate specific consultant characteristics and the usefulness of the service. Anonymous completion reduces social-desirability pressure and fear of exposure, so the feedback is more candid.
Routing feedback through the captain adds a filter and a peer power dynamic, and players may still hold back with a teammate collecting their views.
takeaway: Use structured, anonymous consultant evaluation forms to get candid client feedback on your effectiveness.

stem: After a goal-setting session with a high school track team went poorly, a consultant writes a journal entry. It describes what happened (athletes on their phones, little discussion) and how he felt (frustrated, a bit embarrassed), then ends: "Next time I'll be more engaging." Using Gibbs's reflective cycle, what is the main thing missing from his reflection?
options: A fuller description of the session, including the exact point each athlete disengaged
Judging what went well and poorly, and analyzing why the session unfolded as it did
A stronger account of his feelings so that their emotional impact is fully captured
A plan to share the journal entry with the head coach and the team captains
rationales: He has already described the session; more detail at the description stage does not produce the sense-making the cycle requires.

Gibbs's cycle moves from description and feelings to evaluation (what was good and bad about the experience) and analysis (making sense of it, for example with theory or context), then to a conclusion and a specific action plan. Jumping straight to "be more engaging" leaves the plan vague because he has not worked out why the session failed.
His feelings are already named; dwelling on them further does not address the missing evaluation and analysis stages.
A reflective journal serves the practitioner's own learning; sharing it is not a stage of Gibbs's cycle and could raise confidentiality concerns.
takeaway: Reflection that jumps from feelings to "do better next time" skips evaluation and analysis, the stages that make an action plan specific.

stem: Rosalind, a masters triathlete, has met her goals for managing race-morning worry after four months of work, and she and her consultant agree to end after two more sessions. Her next goal race is overseas, with an unfamiliar course, long travel, and a large time-zone change. Which focus for the final sessions best supports her keeping her gains after consultation ends?
options: Introduce several advanced mental skills so she has more tools available on race day
Schedule monthly check-ins with no end date so any setback can be caught quickly
Readminister her intake questionnaires to document how much she has improved
Identify likely trouble spots at that race and rehearse how she will cope on her own
rationales: Adding new skills at the end dilutes consolidation of the skills that already work and risks sending her off with partly learned tools.
Open-ended scheduled sessions foster dependence and contradict the ending she agreed to; an open-door policy or an optional follow-up is appropriate, but indefinite check-ins are not.
Documenting change is useful for evaluation, but it does not prepare her for the new demands she is about to face.

Planned termination includes generalization and relapse-prevention planning: anticipating high-risk situations, rehearsing self-directed coping for them, and building the client's independence so skills transfer to new settings after consultation ends.
takeaway: Before ending, build independence: anticipate high-risk situations and rehearse self-directed coping so gains generalize.

stem: A consultant spent a season with a collegiate volleyball team that went on to win its conference title. The athletic director wants to announce that the mental training program "won us the championship" and asks the consultant for a supporting quote. During the same season, the team added a transfer setter and overhauled its strength program. How should the consultant respond?
options: Frame the program as one contributor and offer the season's process and behavior data
Provide the requested quote, since winning the title shows the program achieved its purpose
Decline to comment, since mental training outcomes cannot be meaningfully evaluated
Credit the new setter and strength staff instead, to avoid seeming to overstate the program
rationales: A championship is a results-level outcome (Kirkpatrick) with many causes, here including a new setter and a new strength program. Honest evaluation frames the program as a contributor and points to team-level evidence more directly tied to it, such as process and behavior data, which protects the consultant's integrity and credibility.
Claiming sole credit for a multi-causal outcome overstates the evidence and misleads the public, and it sets the program up to look like a failure in a losing season.
Mental training programs can be evaluated meaningfully; refusing to comment gives up a chance to give a key stakeholder accurate evidence.
Swinging to credit others ignores the program's real evidence; the goal is accurate attribution, not modesty.
takeaway: Present outcomes as multi-causal: claim a contribution, not sole credit, and point to the evidence closest to what the program targeted.

stem: A consultant has worked with Tomasz, a conservatory violist preparing for orchestra auditions, on a pre-performance routine. Session logs show he now completes the routine before nearly every mock audition, and his self-rated tension has dropped. The consultant next wants to learn whether Tomasz and his viola teacher regard these changes as worthwhile and the routine as practical in a performer's life. Which evaluation approach addresses this question?
options: Continue logging routine completion for another month to confirm that the trend holds
Administer a validated trait anxiety inventory and compare his score with published norms
Hold social validation interviews with Tomasz and his teacher about the work
Compare his audition results this year with those of other violists at his level
rationales: More of the same data strengthens the evidence that behavior changed, but it cannot capture whether the change matters to Tomasz or his teacher.
A trait inventory compared with norms measures a stable disposition; it does not speak to the practical significance or acceptability of the intervention.

Social validation asks clients and significant others whether the goals were important, the procedures acceptable, and the effects meaningful in everyday performance life. That is exactly the question here, and it complements the behavioral and self-report data already collected.
Audition outcomes compared across violists are confounded by panels, repertoire, and the competition, and they do not ask the stakeholders for their own judgment of the work's value.
takeaway: Social validation asks clients and stakeholders whether goals, procedures, and outcomes were important, acceptable, and meaningful.

stem: Midway through an Olympic cycle, a consultant to a national rowing team reviews anonymous evaluation forms. Athletes rate her as knowledgeable, trustworthy, and easy to talk to, but many add that her sessions are "interesting but hard to use on the water." Based on research on consultant effectiveness with elite athletes, which change should she prioritize?
options: Add more sessions on psychological theory to deepen the athletes' understanding
Turn content into concrete strategies tailored to each rower and practiced in training
Spend less time at practices so athletes come to see her as more of an outside expert
Stop using evaluation forms, since athletes already rate her relationship skills highly
rationales: More theory moves further from the athletes' stated need; being too theoretical and not applied is one of the traits athletes associate with less effective consultants.

Studies of consultant effectiveness with Olympic athletes (Partington and Orlick's evaluation work; Gould and colleagues) found that effective consultants offer clear, practical strategies individualized to the athlete and usable in the sport. The feedback points to exactly that gap.
Effective consultants were described as fitting in with the team and being accessible; pulling back from practices works against helping athletes apply skills on the water.
Strong relationship ratings do not make further feedback unnecessary; the forms have just identified an important gap, and ongoing evaluation is part of effective practice.
takeaway: Elite athletes value consultants who fit in and give practical, individualized strategies they can use in their sport.

stem: A consultant tried a new trust-building activity with a youth hockey team, and it fell flat: players joked through it and the coach cut it short. That evening he reviewed his notes and observed that the activity ran long, came right after a hard skate, and asked 12-year-olds to share personal stories in front of the group. According to Kolb's experiential learning cycle, what should he do next?
options: Run the same activity again next week to see whether the result changes
Ask the coach to rate the activity on a satisfaction scale before deciding
Drop team-building activities, since this group is not ready for that work
Use theory to explain what happened and draft a revised approach to try
rationales: Repeating the identical activity skips a phase; active experimentation should test a revised idea, not the same one that just failed.
Another rating might be useful, but it is not the next phase of the cycle; he already has clear observations to learn from.
Abandoning the approach overgeneralizes from one experience instead of doing the theory-informed sense-making the cycle calls for.

Kolb's cycle runs from concrete experience to reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation. Having reflected on what happened, his next step is to make sense of it conceptually (for example, age-appropriate disclosure, timing, and group development) and form a revised approach to test.
takeaway: In Kolb's cycle, reflection is followed by abstract conceptualization, making sense of the experience with theory, before testing a revised approach.

topic: Ending when the fit is poor
stem: A consultant has met by video with Annika, an elite figure skater, for eight sessions on competition focus. They reviewed progress together at session four and revised the plan, but Annika's ratings and her coach's reports still show little change, and Annika says the cognitive approach "just doesn't click" for her. The consultant's training is mainly in cognitive-behavioral methods. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Discuss ending openly and suggest practitioners whose approaches may fit her better
Continue the current plan, since mental skills development often takes longer than expected
Increase sessions to twice weekly to speed up her progress with the same approach
End the consultation by email to spare Annika an uncomfortable final conversation
rationales: When a client is not benefiting despite a joint review and revision, and the mismatch involves the consultant's approach, ethical practice is to discuss ending openly and help the client find a better-fitting provider. This protects her welfare and respects her autonomy.
Continuing without benefit after a revision has already been tried is not in her interest; "give it more time" ignores both the monitoring data and her direct feedback.
More of an approach that is not working adds time and cost without addressing the problem of fit.
Ending abruptly by email amounts to abandonment; a planned conversation with alternatives offered is the standard for concluding, even when the fit is poor.
takeaway: When a client isn't benefiting after the plan has been revised, discuss ending and help them find a better-fitting practitioner.

stem: A consultant who works with six executives at a financial firm on performing under pressure accepts a position abroad and will stop practicing locally in three months. Two of the executives are midway through their plans and want to keep working on their goals with someone. How should the consultant handle these two clients?
options: Send both clients' files to a trusted colleague now so that the colleague can contact them
Tell them soon, review progress, and with consent arrange a handoff to another consultant
Keep working as usual and tell them about the move during the final week of sessions
Tell the firm's HR director which clients still need help so HR can arrange coverage
rationales: Sending records without consent breaches confidentiality and takes away the clients' choice about whether, and with whom, to continue.

Ending because of the consultant's own circumstances still calls for planned termination: timely notice, a review of progress, and, with each client's consent, a transition to another qualified provider, sharing information only as the client authorizes.
Last-minute notice leaves no time to consolidate gains or arrange continuity, which amounts to an abrupt termination.

Telling the employer which employees are clients and what they need breaches confidentiality unless the clients agreed to it; the firm is a stakeholder but is not entitled to that information by default.
takeaway: When you must end, give timely notice, review progress, and arrange a consented handoff to another provider.

stem: A consultant is introducing a free-throw routine to three wheelchair basketball players in a national-team development squad. She wants evidence that the routine, rather than ordinary practice, drives any improvement, and she records each player's free-throw percentage at every practice. Which way of introducing the routine would best support that inference?
options: Introduce it to all three players at once and compare their averages before and after
Teach it only to the player with the lowest percentage, since change is easiest to see
Start it with each player at a different time, keeping the others in baseline
Ask each player at the end of the month to rate whether the routine helped
rationales: Starting everyone at once is a simple before-and-after comparison; any shared influence that coincides with the start, such as a change in practice or the season calendar, cannot be ruled out.
Choosing the lowest scorer invites regression toward the mean, and a single player with no staggered comparison gives weak evidence.

A multiple-baseline design across participants staggers when the intervention starts. If each player's percentage changes only after the routine is introduced for that player, while players still in baseline stay the same, ordinary practice and shared events become unlikely explanations.
End-of-month ratings capture perceptions, which can add social validation, but they cannot separate the routine's effect from the effect of practice.
takeaway: Staggering the start across individuals (a multiple-baseline design) strengthens causal inference in single-case evaluation.

stem: During a live video workshop on stress management for a fire department's new recruits, a consultant notices that cameras are switching off and the chat has gone quiet ten minutes into her slides. She pauses, asks recruits to type the situations they expect to find most stressful, and builds the rest of the session around their answers. Which concept best describes what she did?
options: Reflection-on-action, reviewing a finished session afterward to plan future changes
Gibbs's action-plan stage, deciding what to do differently in the next workshop
Abstract conceptualization, linking the session to theory in a later journal entry
Reflection-in-action, adjusting her approach while the session was still under way
rationales: Reflection-on-action happens after the event, looking back to learn from it; she changed course during the session itself.
The action-plan stage closes Gibbs's after-the-event cycle by planning for next time; she acted in the moment rather than planning a future session.
Abstract conceptualization in Kolb's cycle is a later step of making sense of an experience with theory; nothing in the scenario happens after the session.

Schön distinguished reflection-in-action, thinking and adjusting while practice is unfolding, from reflection-on-action, reviewing afterward. Noticing disengagement and reshaping the workshop on the spot is reflection-in-action.
takeaway: Reflection-in-action is adjusting during the session; reflection-on-action is the structured review afterward. Skilled consultants use both.

stem: A consultant's season-long contract with a collegiate lacrosse team ends after the final tournament. Over the year she ran team sessions, met with individual athletes, and trained the coaching staff to lead short pre-practice focus routines. The head coach wants those routines to continue next season without her. Which plan best concludes the consultation?
options: Hold a closing team session, prepare staff to lead routines, and agree on follow-up
Give the coach a summary of what each athlete discussed in individual sessions
Stop attending once the tournament ends, since the contract term is over
Teach the team several new advanced skills during the final week to extend its toolkit
rationales: Ending with a team is a planned process: a closing session to review and consolidate, building the staff's capacity so the work is sustainable once the consultant leaves, and an agreed follow-up or open-door arrangement within the contract's terms.
What athletes discussed individually is confidential; any summary for the coach requires each athlete's consent and must match what was agreed at the outset.
Letting the contract lapse without closure leaves no consolidation, no transition to staff, and no follow-up plan.
New skills at the very end dilute consolidation and leave the staff trying to sustain skills that were never established.
takeaway: Conclude team work with a closing session, a handoff of routines to staff, and agreed follow-up, while keeping individual content confidential.

stem: A newly certified consultant reviews end-of-program evaluation forms from three different teams. On all three, athletes rate her strategies as useful but repeatedly comment that she "talks more than she listens" in individual sessions. She does not currently have a supervisor or mentor. What is the most appropriate next step for her professional development?
options: Discount the comments, since athletes on all three teams also rated her strategies useful
Seek peer consultation or mentoring to review her sessions and set a listening goal
Switch to group-only formats, where her talking style is less of a concern
Rate her own listening on the same form and rely on that self-assessment
rationales: Strength in one area does not cancel a consistent concern in another; dismissing repeated feedback defeats the purpose of evaluation.

A theme that recurs across independent evaluations is credible feedback. Taking it to peer consultation or a mentor (for example, reviewing session recordings or detailed case notes with client consent) and setting a concrete skill goal is how practitioners turn evaluation data into reflective, ongoing development.
Avoiding individual work sidesteps the problem instead of developing a core consulting skill, and listening matters in group work too.
Self-ratings are prone to the very blind spots that external feedback exists to reveal; relying on them alone is unlikely to change the pattern.
takeaway: Treat consistent client feedback as data for growth: take it to peer consultation or mentoring and set a specific skill goal.

stem: Darnell, a 45-year-old office manager, is working with a consultant on building a consistent running habit before a charity 10K. His training logs show he met his weekly target for six straight weeks, then dropped to about half of it in weeks seven and eight. Nothing in the plan has changed. What should the consultant do first?
options: Replace the current strategies with a new motivational technique starting this week
Remind Darnell of his commitment and ask him to double his runs next week
Review the logs with Darnell to learn what changed before revising the plan
Treat the drop as normal fluctuation and continue the plan without changes
rationales: Changing strategies before understanding the cause may discard what worked for six weeks and may not address the real barrier.
Pressure and a sudden doubling of volume ignore the reason for the drop and raise the risk of injury and dropout.

Monitoring data signal that something changed but not why. Reassessing collaboratively with the client (for example, a new work schedule, a minor injury, or fading motivation) identifies the barrier so that any revision is targeted and the client stays engaged in the plan.
A sustained two-week halving after six consistent weeks is a meaningful signal; ignoring it wastes the point of monitoring.
takeaway: When monitoring data shift, reassess with the client to learn why before revising the plan.
